Can we use AI with CUI?

Only with systems that meet your safeguarding obligations, and consumer AI tools generally don't. A model hosted inside your assessed environment, or fully air-gapped, keeps CUI within the boundary your system security plan describes.

What's the current CMMC timeline?

As of October 2026, Phase 1 requirements (in effect since November 10, 2025) remain in place, while the Phase 2 third-party assessment rollout was paused in July 2026 pending review. Requirements flow down to subcontractors, so plan as if certification is coming.

Private LLM vs. Cloud AI: A Decision Guide for Regulated Businesses

When does it make sense to run your own language model instead of using a cloud AI service? Five questions, a cost formula and three architectures for firms that handle confidential or regulated data.

By Leverline ResearchPublished October 21, 20266 min read

Short version: for most businesses handling confidential data, the answer is a hybrid. Sensitive, high-volume work runs on a private model you control; the occasional task that truly needs a frontier model goes to a cloud API, redacted and approved. Cost alone rarely justifies private AI for light chat use. Control, compliance and predictable cost at high volume usually do.

Five questions that decide it

1. What data will the AI touch? Public marketing copy carries little risk. Client files, health information, controlled unclassified information (CUI) or privileged legal material change the calculus. If a data-processing agreement or business associate agreement can't cover a cloud provider, or your clients won't accept one, private is the only option.

2. How much volume? A few dozen people chatting occasionally is cheap on any cloud API. Automations that read every invoice, call transcript or support ticket generate a lot of tokens. Hardware is a fixed cost, so private deployment gets cheaper per request as volume grows.

3. How hard are the tasks? Summarizing, extracting fields, classifying and answering questions from your own documents are well within reach of current open-weight models. The hardest multi-step reasoning still favors frontier cloud models.

4. Who will run it? A private model is a system: patching, monitoring, model updates, backups and access control. Budget for a managed service or in-house time.

5. What do clients and contracts require? Outside-counsel guidelines, defense contracts and healthcare partners increasingly specify where data may be processed. Those requirements often decide the question before cost does.

A simple cost comparison

Use your own numbers. Model prices change often.

  • Cloud monthly cost ≈ requests per month × average tokens per request × price per token
  • Private monthly cost ≈ (hardware cost ÷ 36 months) + power and hosting + support

Illustrative example: 60 staff making 40 requests a day at about 3,000 tokens each is roughly 160 million tokens a month. At a blended cloud price of $5 per million tokens, that's about $800 a month. A $25,000 GPU server amortized over three years is about $700 a month before power and support, so on cost alone, cloud wins at this volume. Add a document-processing automation that reads 50,000 pages a month, or compare against per-seat enterprise licenses, and the picture can flip.

The point isn't the exact numbers. It's to run the comparison with your real usage before buying hardware.

Three architectures

  1. Fully private (on-prem or air-gapped). Model, retrieval and interface run on your hardware with no internet connection. Best for CUI, privileged material and strict data-residency rules.
  2. Private cloud (your VPC). Open-weight models on GPU instances inside your own cloud account. Most of the control of on-prem with elastic capacity.
  3. Hybrid with a router. A private model handles sensitive and high-volume work; a routing layer sends approved, redacted requests to a frontier API. This is where most regulated mid-sized firms land.

A practical checklist

  • Classify the data each use case touches before choosing a deployment
  • Benchmark two or three models on your real tasks, not public leaderboards
  • Tie access to existing identity and log every request
  • Document the system in your security program (risk analysis, SSP or WISP)
  • Plan model updates through change control
  • Re-run the cost comparison every six months as prices and models change

SMB AI Adoption in 2026 and Where Demand Goes Next

What the latest Census, Federal Reserve, Gartner and industry surveys say about small-business AI adoption, and our outlook for which AI use cases businesses will fund through 2028.

By Leverline ResearchPublished October 21, 20267 min read

Short version: depending on how you ask the question, somewhere between one in five and three in four US small businesses "use AI." The gap between those numbers is the real story, and the real opportunity. Most businesses have tried AI tools; very few have built AI into the workflows where money is made and lost.

Why adoption numbers disagree

The strictest measure comes from the U.S. Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks whether a business used AI in any business function in the past two weeks. As of May 2026 the national rate was about 19.8%, with the Information (39.7%) and Finance and Insurance (33.9%) sectors well above average. Between December 2025 and May 2026, use rose among firms with 20 or more employees but was flat among smaller firms (Census Bureau).

Broader surveys that count any use of AI tools land much higher. Goldman Sachs' 10,000 Small Businesses Voices survey, fielded in early 2026, found 76% of small businesses use AI in some form, but only 14% have it fully embedded in core operations (summary via Delaware Inc.). Thryv's 2026 survey put adoption at 66%, up from 55% a year earlier, with 70% of owners saying they need more training to use it well (WICPA). Intuit's 2026 AI Impact Report found more than three in four US small and midsize businesses now use AI regularly, led by marketing, admin and customer service (Intuit).

The Federal Reserve noted the same spread: Census data put firm-level adoption around 18% at the end of 2025, while an employment-weighted measure from the Atlanta Fed's Survey of Business Uncertainty was around 78%, because large employers adopt first (Federal Reserve).

The gap: trying AI vs. running on AI

Put those numbers together and a clear pattern emerges:

  • Individual use is common. Owners and staff use chat assistants to draft emails, posts and summaries.
  • Operational use is rare. Few businesses have AI answering their phones, processing their documents, scoring their leads or forecasting their inventory.
  • Skills, not interest, are the bottleneck. Training needs and lack of expertise show up across surveys as the leading barriers.

The bottleneck is implementation: choosing the right workflow, connecting it to existing systems, measuring the result and keeping it working.

Where the money is going

Gartner's September 2026 forecast puts worldwide AI spending at roughly $2.7 trillion for 2026, up about 50% year over year, with infrastructure the largest share (Gartner). Within that, AI services spending is forecast at about $576 billion in 2026 (Techstrong). Earlier in the year Gartner also described AI as sitting in the "trough of disillusionment" through 2026, arguing that ROI must become more predictable before enterprises scale up (Gartner, January 2026).

Larger organizations show the same "pilot to production" problem. McKinsey's 2025 State of AI survey found 88% of organizations use AI in at least one function, but no more than 10% report scaling AI agents in any single function (McKinsey).

Our outlook: what businesses will fund through 2028

This is our view, based on the data above and what we see in the market. Treat it as a planning input, not a prediction.

Use case Demand outlook Why
AI voice agents & receptionists Very strong Revenue-recovery math is simple, deployment takes weeks and costs keep falling.
Document & workflow automation Strong, steady Labor constraints plus agents that can finally handle messy inputs.
Private & local LLMs Rising fast in regulated sectors Confidentiality, HIPAA and CMMC obligations, and capable open-weight models.
Natural-language analytics Rising in the mid-market Snowflake and Databricks ship native tools, but accuracy depends on semantic layers someone has to build.
Lead engines & ad signal work Strong Privacy changes make first-party data and conversion APIs essential.
Governance & training Steady Most owners want training, and regulation is arriving, if slower than expected.
Custom AI products Growing Software companies need AI features that hold up in production and protect margins.

On regulation: the EU's Digital Omnibus moved most high-risk AI Act obligations to December 2027 (Gibson Dunn), and Colorado's AI Act was revised with its effective date pushed to January 2027 (Checkr). Delays buy time; they don't remove the need for basic governance.

What this means if you're deciding where to start

  1. Start where the ROI math is simplest. Missed calls, re-keyed documents and slow lead follow-up have obvious baselines.
  2. Measure before you build. Agree on one success metric and record the baseline first.
  3. Budget for adoption, not just software. Training and change management decide whether a tool becomes a habit.
  4. Keep sensitive data private. If confidentiality is a concern, a private model removes the question entirely.

We design, deploy and maintain private large language models that run on a server in your office, in your own cloud account, or fully air-gapped. Your team gets modern AI without sending client data to a third party.

The problem

Your people are already pasting contracts, financials and customer records into public AI tools, or they're banned from using AI at all and falling behind. Neither is acceptable when you handle confidential or regulated data, and per-seat AI licenses get expensive as usage grows.

How we solve it

We stand up an open-weight model (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma or gpt-oss class) behind a familiar chat interface, connect it to your documents with permission-aware retrieval, and wrap it with logging, access control and usage policies.   3. Deploy and connect

Families Helping a Parent Age in Place · Aging in Place

A Camera-Free Sensor Plan for an Aging Parent

Families often reach for cameras first, and parents often refuse them. A sensor plan gives most of the reassurance with none of the intrusion: it knows the kitchen got used this morning and records no images.

Illustrative scenario

An 82-year-old lives alone in a one-story house; her son lives two hours away. We place motion sensors in the bedroom, hallway, bathroom and kitchen, door sensors on the front door and fridge, and motion-activated path lighting from bed to bathroom. After two weeks of learning her routine, the son gets a text only if the kitchen sees no activity by 10am or the front door opens between midnight and 5am.

  • Give caregivers their own lock codes
  • Keep a medical alert device for emergencies

Worth knowing

  • Sensors don't diagnose anything; they report activity.
  • Too many alerts lead families to ignore them. We tune for few, meaningful alerts.
  • Shared accounts let more than one family member help.

HomeInsightsAutomatic Water Shutoff Valves: Cost, Savings and Insurance Discounts

October 26, 2026 · 5 min read

Automatic Water Shutoff Valves: Cost, Savings and Insurance Discounts

Short version: a whole-home automatic shutoff valve with leak and freeze sensors costs roughly $1,500 installed in a typical home in our price list. It's one of the few smart-home upgrades whose value comes from avoiding a very large bill, and some insurers now discount premiums for it.

Why water is the risk to plan for

State Farm reported more than 20,000 frozen-pipe claims from January 2024 through June 2025, totaling over $628 million in paid losses, with an average claim payment above $30,000 (Carrier Management, January 2026). Burst pipes are only one source; supply lines, water heaters, washers and dishwashers fail too, often when nobody is home.

How an automatic shutoff works

A valve on the main water line measures flow. When it sees a pattern that looks like a burst or a leak, or a linked sensor detects water, it closes the main line and alerts your phone. Installing the valve is plumbing work on the main line, which most areas require a licensed plumber to do.

What it costs with us

Our Safe & Dry package includes the valve, six leak sensors, two freeze sensors and a hub, installed and tested. See the current price on our packages page; older homes or hard-to-reach mains cost more.

Estimating the value honestly

There's no single right number, so use your own inputs:

  • Chance of a serious leak in a year: depends on the home's age, plumbing, climate and how often it's empty. We use 2% as an illustrative default, not a statistic.
  • Typical cost of one: your deductible plus anything not covered, and the disruption. State Farm's frozen-pipe average was above $30,000; we default to a more conservative $15,000.
  • Share prevented: a valve doesn't stop every drip, but it stops the long-running leaks that cause the biggest losses.
  • Insurance discount: varies by insurer and state, from none to a meaningful percentage.

Our savings calculator runs this with your numbers.

Insurance discounts in 2026

Programs are spreading but uneven. In July 2026, Stand Insurance and Moen launched a program in California and Florida that gives premium discounts to policyholders who activate and maintain a Flo shutoff device, and waives a water endorsement requirement for some older homes (Coverager). Ask your agent what your carrier offers and what documentation it needs; we provide an installation record for insurers.

What about tax credits?

The federal 25C energy-efficient home improvement credit ended for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, and it never covered water shutoff valves. Check your water utility and insurer instead.

Is Professional Smart Home Installation Worth It?

Short version: install a smart plug or a battery leak sensor yourself. Hire a professional for anything that touches line-voltage wiring or your water main, for a system of more than a handful of devices that needs to work together, and for a network that has to reach every room.

What homeowners actually do

Parks Associates' quarterly survey of 8,000 US internet households found that 81% of smart-home owners have tried installing at least one device themselves, 44% have used a professional for at least one installation, and about 29% of people who start on their own end up calling a professional (CE Pro, October 2025; SecurityInfoWatch, September 2025). Configuration and setup problems are among the top three reasons devices go back to the store, and professionally installed cameras scored a higher Net Promoter Score (49) than self-installed ones (41) in the same research.

Where DIY works well

  • Plug-in devices: smart plugs, speakers, battery sensors
  • A single device that lives in its own app
  • Homes with strong Wi-Fi and a household that enjoys tinkering

It learns your normal water use, so showers, irrigation and laundry don't trigger it. If it ever closes by mistake, you reopen it from the app or with the manual lever.
